title: Count the Vowels
statement:
Every language track needs a "read a string, look at each character" warm-up,
and counting vowels is the plainest version of it: no data structure to pick,
no algorithm to choose, just the discipline of getting the character
comparison right for every character the string can actually contain.

## Your function

```
public static int CountVowels(string text);
```

Return how many of `text`'s characters are one of `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u`.
`text` may be empty, and is never `null`.

## Watch out

- **`text` can contain upper-case letters.** `"Crucible"` has three: the two
  `i`s aren't there, but the `u`, the first `i`, and the... count them
  yourself, and check your function agrees. The point is that upper-case
  vowels are still vowels -- comparing only against lower-case letters
  quietly undercounts every string that has any capitals in it at all,
  which in ordinary English text is most of them.
- **`y` is never a vowel here.** English usage genuinely disagrees about
  `y` (compare "myth" and "boy"), so this exercise sidesteps the argument
  entirely: the five letters above are the whole list, and `y` -- upper or
  lower case -- is not one of them.
- **Punctuation, digits and spaces are not errors.** They are simply not
  vowels, and the loop should pass over them the same way it passes over
  a consonant -- no special-casing, no exception, just characters that do
  not match.

tests.name: an empty string has no vowels
every letter in the alphabet, lower case
tests.description: Exactly a, e, i, o, u -- five vowels among 26 letters.

tests.name: the same alphabet, upper case
tests.description: Upper-case vowels count too -- a solution that only checks lower case undercounts this to 0.

tests.name: mixed case in an ordinary sentence
tests.description: CRUCIBLE: u, i, e. 'The Quick Brown Fox': e, u, i, o, o.

tests.name: y is never counted as a vowel
punctuation and digits are simply not vowels
tests.description: Only the 'o' in 'go' is a vowel.
